moves.what: a fleeting glance by the character into the lens mid-scene — a smirk, an eyebrow raise, a deadpan face, a shrug or a short line to the viewer — and straight back into the action; the viewer becomes an accomplice
speaking to the audience: the subject turns to the lens to explain, point something out or lean in, and the viewer is pulled into the conversation instead of watching from outside
the borders of the edit become things to touch: bars pried apart, a divider line shoved aside, an image that tears like paper, a frame edge used as a ramp

the camera stops being invisible — the character reaches for it, covers it with a palm, grabs, pushes away, kicks or carries it off, and the world leaves marks on the lens glass (splashes, dirt, drops, a crack, a drawing); the viewer feels they are standing right inside the scene
aliases: cover the lens with a palm

moves.what: a view straight down from a great height — people and cars turn into dots with shadows, the ground into a map or a pattern; the hero dissolves in the scale, the viewer watches with detachment
a shot filmed with the camera rolled 10–35° — the horizon and verticals are visibly tilted; the world is "off-kilter", the viewer feels anxiety, madness or pressure
the camera right at the ground (10–60 cm) looks almost horizontally — the floor or the ground at the bottom of the frame, shoes, feet, a ball, wheels in focus; the world from floor level

the camera is above the hero's eyes and looks down at 15–75° — the hero is smaller and "below" the viewer, with the floor or the ground behind instead of the horizon; an angle of vulnerability, submission or overview
the camera is below the hero's eyes and looks up at 10–45° — the hero towers over the viewer against the sky, a ceiling or stage lights; an angle of power, threat, triumph and monumentality

a view from directly above — the camera above the hero or the scene looks straight down; there is no horizon, the floor or the ground lies in the plane of the frame, and the scene reads as a diagram, a pattern or a map
a close-up framed like a map of the work surface, lens pointing straight down from arm's length: everything lies flat and reads as a diagram; the standard insert for step-by-step, hands-on content

the camera, pointing straight down, travels with the hero, a car or along a row of objects — the floor or the ground flows under the frame, the subject stays in the center; movement across a "map" that instantly shows the layout of the space

the hero filmed strictly from the side — the face reads as the line of forehead, nose, lips and chin; the gaze leaves the frame, the hero seems absorbed in thought and the frame graphic; good for silhouettes, rides, contemplation and models

a view from below, from inside a trunk, a box or a pit — the lid rises out of blackness, 1–5 people loom over the lens and look straight inside, a dark frame of the opening around the edges; an angle of threat, conspiracy or the "what's inside" reveal

the camera lies right on the surface of the water — the waterline cuts the frame, ripples right at the lens, a swimmer's head, a boat or a hand at the viewer's eye level; sometimes a wave washes over the lens or the frame is split into "above" and "below" the water

the camera lies on the ground or the floor and looks almost straight up — people loom over the lens against the sky or a ceiling, heads in a circle or upside down; the "you are lying down and above you…" angle
aliases: camera on the ground looking up
circle of heads over the camera

moves.what: an insert made entirely by a video generator — an impossible scene, a painterly style or a continuous flow of shapes with no cuts (a figure becomes a beast, a cave drawing becomes a fresco); the main tell is a world that "swims"

a stretch of the video in the manner of a hand-drawn cartoon — flat characters with clean outlines over a painted background, drawings change on twos or threes; an insert, a stylization or a meaningful "escape into a cartoon"
an insert of 3D computer animation — an object or character with soft volumetric light, smooth materials and true perspective; a motion-design loop, a simulation or "impossible physics"
monochrome charcoal or chalk animation — every frame is redrawn, the strokes "boil", tone is smudged, traces of erased phases stay visible; a heavy, intimate, anxious mood
characters and a world made of plasticine, animated frame by frame — soft rounded shapes, fingerprints, a "breathing" surface and jerky motion on twos; warm handmade naivety or absurdity
animation in colored pencil, wax crayon or marker — strokes and paper grain are visible, outlines "boil", drawings change on twos or threes; warm, handmade, "straight from a sketchbook"

animation in the language of comics and manga — stark black-and-white drawing with screentone shading, speed lines, a strobing background and panel inserts; turns the action into a drawn scene from a comic
simple drawn faces, eyes, eyebrows and little arms tracked onto an object in live video — the thing "comes alive" and reacts; a comedy device for short videos
animation in a single line without fills — a one-color outline on a solid background; from minimalist loops and portraits to line-drawn panoramas; a clean graphic "pen drawing"
mixed media: hand-made characters and lines join the real scene and react to the person in it
aliases: drawn characters in the real world

moves.what: a still building, facade or street object starts moving like an animation — window modules travel in a loop, floors sway, a column shuffles its segments, a kiosk bends like rubber, a house grows and folds back; meanwhile the camera and sky stay still

a mural or graffiti painted on a wall comes alive in its own painted style — colors run along stripes, a character moves, a portrait changes faces, the painted world interacts with the real one; the wall, building and street stay real
every frame is made of oil-paint brushstrokes — a living painting where the brush texture "boils" from frame to frame, or a filter turns video into a moving canvas; sensual, warm, arthouse
animation in fine graphite or pen on paper — thin lines, hatching and construction lines are visible, every drawing is redrawn and slightly "boils"; a light, handmade, "from a notebook" look

real people shot frame by frame like stop-motion puppets — the body jumps from pose to pose, the subject glides down the street without taking steps, things around crawl and fly on their own, the face changes grimaces in jerks

a short motion loop laid out around a disc — 10–16 phases of one pose cycle across the sectors; the disc turns by exactly one sector per frame and the figures "come alive" in place; a hypnotic retro loop

live footage redrawn frame by frame — people move and act for real but look like a drawing (flat tones with outlines or thick paint); facial expressions and body movement are real, the texture is drawn
a stylization of early black-and-white cartoons — characters and objects brought to life, with jointless hose arms, white gloves and "pie-cut" eyes, bounce to the music all the time over aged film
quick hand-drawn lines, loops, strokes and text over live video or a photo — every frame is redrawn from scratch, so the drawing "boils" and trembles; energy, chaos, a handmade punk delivery

frame-by-frame shooting of real objects, puppets or people — everything is moved by hand between shots, and on playback things "move by themselves"; a handmade jerky rhythm on twos without motion blur
flat vector animation — clean geometric shapes filled with 2–5 colors, hard edges, smooth tweens and shapes flowing into one another; an illustration insert, an explanation or a product stylization
animation in transparent washes of watercolor or ink on white paper — soft patches, bleeds, lots of air; a light, dreamy, poetic mood

bringing a sequence of phases to life — figurines on a spinning drum or carousel, frames seen through slits, or copies of the subject in successive poses add up to a short motion loop; a retro "pre-cinema" motif and a transition into that loop

a sideways arc around the subject at a fixed radius: the background sweeps past while the subject holds the middle of the frame — anything from a slow, tender half-circle to a fast arc in an action beat

the camera travels a full circle around the subject (270–360° and more) in one continuous move — the subject stays in the center of the frame while the world behind spins all the way round; back → face → back, "the whole world around one person" and a view from every side

the camera travels along an arc in the vertical plane around the subject — from eye level up through a straight top-down view, sometimes further "over the head" so the world turns upside down; a striking change of viewpoint on a single object
the camera travels strictly up or down without tilting — it rises from behind the foreground, descends to the characters or moves from floor to floor

a long smooth camera move on a telescoping arm — over tables, a sofa, a crowd, through a window or a door; in a single move the camera changes both height and distance, leading from a wide view right to the hero or revealing the space on a pull-out

smash cut — at the peak of a jolt (a sharp push-in or pull-out) the shot breaks off and crashes into a contrasting world (from a crowd to a quiet landscape, from darkness to color, from macro to a top-down view); the new shot flies out of the same motion and brakes to a standstill within 0.25–0.55 s

editing and camera serve the dance — a shot holds a whole movement phrase, the camera either stays still so the group's pattern reads or follows the body's trajectory, and cuts, light and effects hit the movement accents and the beats

a stream of dozens of different images at 1–2 frames each (12–25 changes per second) — most often the eyes, face, figure or object stay at one point of the frame while people, places, outfits and color flicker around them; energy, "the whole collection in a couple of seconds", a flash of memory

a cut from a wide or medium shot to a tighter shot of the same place and moment — a face, a hand, an object or a detail of the action; the action is not interrupted, and the viewer gets a "magnifying glass" on what matters

a cut within one camera setup with a chunk of time removed — the background stays put while the subject's pose, position or surroundings change in a jump; it compresses speech and action, shows that time has passed, sets a nervous rhythm

a cut in which two different shots share the main thing — the shape, the subject's pose and position, an object or the composition; the world around changes while the eye sees continuity and a "rhyme"

a burst of 3–20 short shots in a row, 2–15 frames @25 fps each (0.07–0.6 s) — each holds one action, detail or face, the cuts hit the beats or the hits of the action, and the burst usually discharges into a long held shot

the motion "gets stuck" — a 3-frame fragment repeats 7–9 times in a row (about a second), a run, a gesture or a swing twitches in place at ≈8 Hz, then comes a cut, or the motion is released and carries on

cutting on the motion vector — the end of shot A and the start of shot B move in the same direction (a pan, a tilt, a push-in or pull-out, a roll, the subject itself), so different places and times read as one continuous move; the speed at the seam is held, damped or accelerated

the camera with a wide-angle lens physically lunges at the face in a fraction of a second — the face grows from a wide shot to an extreme close-up and is distorted by perspective, while the background barely grows; often it springs right back, like a hit on the rhythm

the subject stands or sits on the same dolly as the camera and "floats" through space without walking — their shot size and position in the frame don't change while the street, corridor or crowd is carried away behind; a feeling that the subject is carried by fate, a thought or the music

the camera glides smoothly, without tracks, toward or away from the subject at walking speed — like a dolly, but it passes through doors, crowds, stairs and windows; a light "floating" feel and real parallax

the camera physically travels toward the subject (or away from them) steadily and slowly — the face grows faster than the background, the perspective changes; a push-in draws attention inward to the subject, a pull-out reveals where they are and who they are with
the camera travels forward (or backward) through a space that never ends — a corridor, an arcade, a row of trees or seats repeats, and the movement is looped or cut together so the seam isn't visible

the subject keeps the same shot size while the space behind them stretches or compresses — the camera travels one way, the zoom works the other way; "the ground slips from under the feet", shock, realization, a shift of reality

filming from the air — a drone or helicopter flies smoothly high above a city, nature or a road — reveals the place, follows a car or a boat, flies away from the subject or dives toward them; the main establishing shot and a link between locations
a rapid flight of a light drone right next to surfaces — banking into turns, diving along walls and flipping over, in a single 3–10 second take
within one continuous shot the main subject changes — focus, camera or blocking lead the viewer's eye from character A to character or object B without an edit cut
out-of-focus point lights turn into soft glowing discs — a background behind the character, an abstract backdrop, or a transition through defocus
within one shot the plane of focus travels from one subject to another — the foreground blurs, the background turns sharp (or vice versa); guides the eye without a cut
shallow depth of field — only the character or object is sharp, the foreground and background are softly blurred; isolates the subject and guides the eye without editing
a half lens keeps two planes sharp at once — a close-up face at the edge of the frame and a distant figure in the other half; a soft vertical seam between them

a sharp horizontal band across the middle of a high-angle wide shot, everything above and below smoothly blurred, colors saturated, motion sped up — a real city or landscape looks like a toy scale model
composition on the central axis — the subject exactly in the middle, the surroundings mirror-symmetric, the horizon level; a "statement" frame that stops the eye

a person answers an unseen interviewer — the gaze goes past the lens toward the interviewer, the face sits on a third with looking room in the direction of the gaze; the backbone of documentary and explainer editing

over-the-shoulder shot — the subject in focus is filmed from behind the other person; that person's blurred back of the head and shoulder cover a third of the frame on one side, and the subject looks toward them; the basis of shot/reverse-shot dialogue and a way to show what a character sees without taking them out of the frame
a still, carefully built frame like a painting — the camera stands still, people pose or barely move within a deliberate composition and palette, and the frame is viewed like a canvas
two people in one frame — side by side facing the camera, facing each other, or one closer and the other in depth; the characters' relationship, distance and inequality are visible without a cut
a peeping shot — the subject doesn't know they are being watched; we see them from afar through a gap, a window, a fence, a scope or binoculars, and most of the frame is covered by a dark obstruction
a person's live head is out of proportion to the body — the head is enlarged or the body shrunk to a child's or doll's size; an adult turns into a living toy, a comedic composite
aliases: adult head on a child's body

moves.what: the scene's color changes abruptly or smoothly right inside a shot or on a cut — per-channel monotone, a drop to B&W and the return of color, a "creeping" hue, a different light color on the same scene — as an accent on the beat or on a change of meaning

the same person or object appears in the frame several times — a double at the table, a hall full of clones, copies popping up on the beats, an object multiplied into a forest or a flock; the scene is whole, without borders or seams

a procedural film texture over any shot — grain, dust, hairs, scratches, flicker and frame micro-weave — with no change of color, frame border or format; from a barely noticeable "organic" feel to old film, in levels 1–3
short bursts of a "broken" digital picture — slices slide sideways, color channels separate, rows smear, the frame inverts or sticks — and then immediately a clean image again
bright areas of the frame spill into a soft glow of their own color — from a light dreamy sheen to a neon halo; constant over an episode or as a pulse on the beat

the frame folds into a symmetrical pattern — sectors with mirrored copies around the center, mirror tiles or a "tunnel"; the pattern slowly rotates and breathes with zoom, turning any footage into a mandala

black bars smoothly slide onto the frame or off it — the aspect ratio changes right in the shot (16:9 ↔ 2.2–2.4:1, ↔ 4:3, slit ↔ full frame) to "switch on cinema", open or close a scene, move to another time

warm patches of light drift in from the frame edge and slowly float over the picture, independent of its content — a soft "filmic" glow over an episode or a transition where the cut hides inside a flared-up patch

an inanimate object gets a face and a personality — eyes, a mouth, facial expressions, a pose and a voice; a stone blinks, a power socket looks surprised, a ball sings, a mountain smiles; comedy, cuteness and a mascot out of any object
for censorship, anonymity or a joke, one object in live footage is covered with a mosaic of large squares — the subject seems to turn into a character from an old video game
the frame as seen through a night vision device — green monochrome with grain, dark edges or a round eyepiece, glowing eyes and bloomed lights; the aesthetic of surveillance, hunting, found footage

360-camera footage unwrapped into an unusual projection — the whole sphere as a flat strip, an ultra-wide "ball", a tunnel, or an orbit around the subject from an invisible stick; the frame bends and spins in ways a normal camera cannot

the whole frame is drawn (or converted) in large square pixels with a reduced palette and no anti-aliasing, and motion steps at 7–17 drawings per second — the aesthetic of old video games — cozy pixel dioramas, character and mascot sprites, game scenes with a game UI
another video falls as light onto a face, a body, fabric, palms, water mist or a stage backdrop — the image bends over the relief, darkness all around; a ghostly, dreamy, theatrical image

the frame contains a smaller copy of itself where a picture would naturally sit — on a phone screen, in a photo, in a frame, in a mirror — the copy contains the next one, and so on down to a point; zooming into the copy returns to the start and makes an endless loop
aliases: frame within a frame within a frame

moves.what: the picture "through glass" — a prism multiplies parts of the frame and splits them into a rainbow, fluted glass slices it into vertical strips, heat haze ripples the bottom of the frame, soft edges stretch into a smear; the story stays readable in the center
aliases: glass in front of the lens

moves.what: the frame's R, G and B channels briefly slide apart and immediately come back together — outlines grow red and cyan fringes; a "digital hit" on the beat, a punch or a cut, with the frame geometry intact

an object, a person or a place is shown as a scanned 3D model — it hangs on a gray "software screen", rotates on a turntable, breaks down into a wireframe or a point cloud, and the camera flies inside the model

each row or column of the frame shows its own moment in time — motion turns into twisted, stretched, "rubbery" shapes while static things stay normal; plus a variant with the background unrolled into stripes
an animal speaks with a human voice — the mouth, beak or fish lips open syllable by syllable, the head nods on stressed syllables; from a pet's "inner monologue" to puppet animals in human clothes
the frame in a thermal imager's palette — cold is black-violet, warm is orange, people and skin glow yellow-white; a soft "sensor" image, a feeling of surveillance or animal vision

the whole surround view is wrapped into a small planet-ball — the ground in the center, sky all around, the subject standing on top; or the reverse, a "hole" — a circle of sky in the center, the ground as walls around it; the planet slowly rotates

the camera flies freely through a frozen moment reconstructed in 3D — people are frozen mid-action, dust and shards hang in the air, and at the edges the frame stretches into radial rays and "swims" — a digital, dreamlike presentation

time freezes while the viewpoint rocks back and forth between 2–4 neighboring angles — the subject stays in place, the background and foreground "float" around them, the volume reads without 3D glasses
the frame becomes an x-ray image — a black background, a translucent cold-blue body through which the bones and skull glow; an eerie or "inner" look at the subject

a callout — a dot with a leader line, an arrow, an outline ring, target brackets or a darkened surround latches onto an object in the frame and labels it with a short fact; it stays on the object via tracking and appears exactly when the object is mentioned, or on a beat

the frame is assembled from cut-out photos, video windows and stickers — pieces land in layers, slightly rotated, with paper borders, tape and shadows, and change in jerks like stop-motion; a handmade, "magazine" feel

counter and infographics — a number counts up to its total, slowing toward the end, bars grow from a common baseline, a chart line draws itself, a ring fills; the total lands exactly on a beat or on the spoken number word
a device interface (messages, a chat, a typing window) hangs right in the scene next to the subject — you see both the face and what they are reading or writing, without cutting away to the screen

live video is mixed in one frame with foreign layers — "machine vision" labeling, interfaces, handwritten marks, print texture, 3D elements; each layer has its own texture and its own pace, and the frame looks assembled rather than shot

a route on a map — the path line is drawn in code from point to point over a solid background or a stylized map, place pins pop up on arrival, a running dot or a transport icon leads the eye, labels are set in our own font; each leg starts on a beat and lands on a downbeat

a hand in the frame controls reality like a phone screen — a swipe flips through scenes, a pinch zooms in, a tap opens, a finger scrolls the frame like a feed, a snap turns day into night; the edit and the graphics fire exactly in time with the gesture

a codec melt — the picture does not refresh at the cut or loops one motion, and the pixels of the old frame flow in 8–16 px blocks along the motion of the new one; scenes bleed into each other without a clean join

imitation of damaged motion-picture film — light leaks and burns, flicker, dust and scratches, a slipped frame with the frame line and sprocket holes; works as the texture of an episode and as a transition

pixel sort — inside the bright (or dark) areas of the frame the pixels of each column or row are re-sorted by brightness, and the picture "drips" in straight gradient streaks; a glitch-art accent on a hit or the texture of an episode
a picture like on an old CRT television with a weak signal — scanlines and a cold screen as the base, and on top — snow, line ripple, vertical roll, loss of sync and "channel switching"
a picture "from a tape and a consumer camcorder" — a soft image with bleeding color, a skewed balance, a noise band at the edge of the frame and tracking glitches, a 4:3 frame, abrupt handheld zooms
the camera is in the operator's hands — the frame constantly "breathes", sways and chases the action; it gives a sense of presence, reportage and nervous energy

the frame is assembled along straight seams from parts of different shots, aligned so that together they form one object — a face from two people, a body from two dancers, day and night of one view, one strike from two sports; a "match cut", only in space rather than in time

the frame is divided into halves, strips or rectangles from different takes with no borders or gaps — the parts butt up against each other and add up to one "almost seamless" picture — two people in one bed, a face from pieces of different takes, a stadium with a player pasted in
a screen glows inside the scene — a TV, a monitor, a phone, a laptop — and shows another video; "media within media", the subject watches or films, archive footage or a broadcast in the room

the whole frame is a device screen (a desktop, a browser, a messenger, a feed, a phone camera, a stream with chat, a terminal), and the story is told through actions in the interface — taps, the cursor, pop-up windows, scrolling and typing

the screen is divided by a thin line or gap into 2–6 windows, each with its own shot, all running at the same time — parallel action, a comparison, a phone call, different times; windows can slide in, rearrange and rotate the border
the shot doesn't fill the whole screen but sits as a window on a solid field (black or white) — lots of empty space around, a feeling of a photograph, an archive, a screen or a private moment

an ultra-wide lens with barrel distortion — the center bulges, straight lines bend near the edges, the image is often inscribed in a circle with black margins; it brings energy, closeness and a "street" or anxious subjectivity

a magnifying glass in the frame — inside the circle the area is magnified 1.6–2.5 times and slightly bulging, outside it the scale is normal; it reads a clue, text or a detail, or comically blows up an eye and a mouth

a thin tube lens, centimeters above a surface or inside an object, glides smoothly through a tiny world — grains, flowers, a table with food, a pocket, a bottle neck — at macro scale and yet with deep focus

an ultra-wide lens without barrel distortion (straight lines stay straight) right up close to the subject — the foreground is huge, the background far and small, the edges stretched, the space "inflates"; energy, comedy, scale
the frame edges darken to black, leaving a round or oval "window" — focus on the center, a look through a tube, a scope, a peephole, a memory or anxiety
the light inside the frame flashes, blinks or strobes — the scene is seen in bursts, without a cut; gives alarm, club energy or a "flash" on a hit
a film-like glow around bright points and edges — a narrow white glow and a wider red-orange halo; makes a digital picture look "filmic" and warm
light from a small bright source — sharp shadow edges, deep shadows and clipped highlights; gives the frame tension, a graphic quality and an "expensive" fashion look
the air in the frame becomes visible — a bright veil lifts the blacks, dampens saturation and contrast, light spreads and draws rays; a dreamy, nostalgic or mystical tone
the cast shadow becomes the main thing in the frame — on the ground or a wall it replaces the hero, doubles them or draws a pattern; mystery, graphics, the plasticity of movement
backlight turns the hero into a black outline — against a bright opening (a window, a door, a sunset, a white wall) only the shape reads; mystery, anonymity, the plasticity of movement
a pool or a cone of light picks out the hero, everything around falls into darkness — isolation, "on stage", emerging from the dark

a deliberately "cheap" look for irony — an obvious chroma key with a pasted-in background, stickers and stock inserts with no disguise, on-the-nose transitions and out-of-the-box effects, the subject in the center plays straight to camera
a "waking dream" look — a faded, soft pastel image of empty familiar places with one impossible detail (sky behind a door, a pool inside a building, a portal), almost no movement
an intoxication look — the frame sways and floats unevenly, the edges are blurred and darkened, the image doubles, sometimes "blinks" to black
a dystopian look — a cold, almost colorless concrete-gray image with a single warm accent (fire, signal smoke), identical figures and masks; static "watching" wide shots alternate with handheld chaos
aliases: gray concrete with a red accent

moves.what: an old motion-picture film look — color grain, flicker and frame jitter, the edges of the film gate with sprocket holes, dust and scratches, flashes and burns at the start and end of the video
a look of excess — the frame is densely packed with objects, patterns, layers and frames in a saturated multicolor palette; not a single empty spot, everything repeats and overlaps
a TV news stylization — broadcast graphics (a headline bar, a ticker, a live badge, a placeholder channel logo) over a reporter stand-up, a press scrum or a "live" wide shot

still photos are inserted into the video as physical prints — with a white border, a tilt and a shadow they drop into a stack, flash by as a slideshow at half a second each, lie as newspaper clippings; live video and photos alternate, giving a sense of memory, an archive or a photo shoot
an "altered perception" look over any shot — an oversaturated split tone, "breathing" and floating surfaces, sway, trails behind movement and color cycling; dosed in levels 1–3

on-screen graphics "straight from 80s–90s TV" — teleshopping plates with a price and a phone number, early 3D graphics with chrome and a checkered floor, glowing vector lines on black — over a 4:3 tape image

the same shot is shown at different stages — the raw plate (a green or blue background, tracking markers, wires), a gray "clay" render, a wireframe, rough animation, the final — and the stages are switched with a wipe, a dissolve or a cut; the viewer sees how the shot was made
the look of an old videotape and an amateur camcorder — a 4:3 frame, a soft image with smeared and shifted color, noise, interference bands and on-screen display text; a "found footage" feel
the video looks like a game — a third-person camera behind the subject's back, a clean "rendered" image, interface icons in the corners, editing with "teleports" between locations
deliberately "amateur" creepy absurdity — faces and bodies cut out with hard edges on a pastel or acid-flashing background, early 3D graphics, googly eyes, low resolution and a choppy frame rate

the video or a fragment is looped — the last frame flows seamlessly into the first, and the picture goes round and round with no visible beginning or end; the loop is built with a recursive zoom-in, a pass through a repeating space, a procession or a process that ends where it began

the subject is cut out of their shot and placed on a different background — a landscape, an interior, outer space, a rushing road; the background can be swapped to the rhythm, and a "cheap" chroma key can be played as a deliberate device

the silhouette of a person or an animal on a light background with a second shot showing through inside it — a forest, a city, a road, foliage; the facial features remain semi-transparent — an image of the "inner world"
the silhouette of a person, face or object becomes a window — inside it another video, a texture or a color, outside it the original shot or a frozen photo; a surreal collage-style accent

ready-made "windows" inside the frame — glass, grid cells, horizontal strips — become masks for another video — time flies by outside the window, the cells of a fence fill up with pictures, strips join different shots by one shape
the camera is static while the subject or object slowly turns on a platform in front of it — a view from all sides against a static background
the camera stays in place and rotates horizontally — it follows a moving subject, shifts the view from one character to another, or reveals the space
the camera stands in the center of a circle of people (a table, a car interior, a room) and rotates in place, showing each person in turn — smoothly around the circle or in snaps from face to face
aliases: camera at the center of the table

moves.what: a glance away and back: after a short look at something beside the subject, the camera settles on its exact first framing again
a lightning-fast sideways turn of the camera within one scene — the frame breaks into horizontal motion blur and half a second later settles on another subject in the same space
a pair or a series of whip pans in opposite directions — the camera snaps to B, holds briefly and returns to A with the same whip, or darts between faces
a still image (a photo, an illustration, a poster) is cut into 2–5 depth layers, and a virtual camera moves so that near layers travel faster than far ones — a flat picture gains volume
the camera flies into an opening, glass, a screen or even into the subject and comes out the other side — in a new space, and at the moment of passing 3–8 dark or blurred frames hide the cut
a "pet's-eye" view — the camera at a height of 20–60 cm trots along, people are visible up to the waist or lean straight down to the lens; the world from below, from the animal's side

the other person looks and speaks straight into the lens because the lens is another character's eyes; the viewer becomes the one being addressed and receives an order, a toast, a confession or a threat
the camera becomes the character's eyes — their hands enter the frame from below, the frame sways in time with the steps and turns like a head; the viewer "lives through" the action themselves
the viewer sits behind the glass: someone getting ready or rehearsing meets the lens eye to eye, though in their world it is their own reflection
the lens stands in for an everyday thing (say, a fridge or a bag), so whoever is busy with it ends up meeting the viewer eye to eye

the camera stands in place of a screen (a phone, a monitor, a scoreboard) — the person looks into the lens while a mirrored semi-transparent interface glows over their face, as if we were looking from inside the glass

a bottle or a flacon stands strictly in the center, label to the camera, and the whole background is its flavor or ingredient (apples, peaches, honeycomb, leaves) in one color; flavors change via falling or sliding ingredients, the ending is a lineup of flavors in stripes

a studio "portrait" of a car — a dark hall with a huge softbox above the car, a camera on a robotic arm glides in an arc from a headlight, a door handle or a running light to the whole car; signature lighting, body lines, details

shots where the product is the hero — a macro detail, a full reveal, a feature in action, the product in hand or in its own "world", a final packshot; a clean background, a slow camera, light tracing the contour

footwear as the hero — a camera right at the ground follows walking feet, a sneaker in hand in close-up, a cut-out pair spins in jerks on a colored background; the rhythm of the steps and the sole are the main accent
we see the character in a mirror — the mirror becomes a frame within the frame; talking to oneself, a double, the "true face", watching from the outside
the character is shown not directly but through a reflection — in water, a puddle, a glossy floor, metal, a lens or glass; a double, an upside-down world, a view "from the outside"

the character is filmed through glass (a car window, a shop window, an apartment window) — reflections of the street, trees, lights slide across the face; two layers of the world in one frame, pensiveness and the road
the camera is rigidly mounted on the subject's body — their face or the back of their head stays locked in frame while the whole world around sways, tilts and drifts; a move about an inner state
a chosen point — an object, a face, a ball — stays dead still in one spot of the frame while the whole world around it slides, spins and scales
the camera is rigidly mounted on a moving object — a hood, a door, a tool, a cart; part of the object stays dead still in frame while the whole world rushes, glides or tumbles around it

a camera on a high-speed robot arm performs, in half a second, a move no camera operator could — an orbit, a swoop from top to bottom, a lunge at a detail with a roll — and freezes exactly on the frame, with no jitter or overshoot
the subject and the camera rotate together on one platform — the person is frozen in the center of the frame while the room or the city races around behind them
aliases: subject and camera on a turntable

moves.what: the camera rotates around the lens axis — the horizon tips over and the world turns 90–180°, or even makes a full revolution; disorientation, a dream, a passage into an "upside-down" world
a rapid roll of the camera around the lens axis by 70–180° over 0.3–0.5 s with motion blur — the frame "flips" and settles in a new position, or twists into a blur and leads out of the scene
inserting real old material — newsreels, educational films, home movies and tapes, old photographs — as context, a memory or a rhythmic montage inside a modern video

a real scale model — a model of a building, a cutaway dollhouse, toy soldiers, toy cars, a figurine in a music box — filmed either as the real world or openly as a model; gives a fairy-tale feel, a "handmade" quality and ironic distance
a fall of a person, an object or the camera itself — accelerating downward, with wind in the hair, a tumble in the void or a plunge into darkness; loss of control, a dream, a climax and the "drop"
a person, a vehicle or an object flies through the air under control — takes off, speeds over the ground, soars in the wind toward the clouds; freedom, superpowers, a dream, humor

an optical trick on a static camera — a near and a far object are aligned at one point of the frame, and the brain reads them as the same scale; a person "picks up" a car with two fingers, "steps" on a street, drops a potato that lands as a boulder

a person, an animal or an object the size of a mountain towers over the ordinary world — waist-deep behind hills, in the clouds or in haze, with tiny people and cars at its feet; the shot sells scale, dread or epic grandeur

a person or an object hangs or slowly drifts in the air without visible support — feet a few centimeters above the floor, a body above a bed or a crowd, an object under a streetlight; magic, a dream, superpowers, weightlessness

a shot of an empty transitional space — a corridor, a staircase, a pool, an enfilade of arches or columns — in a single color, with the vanishing point in the center and an even, slow tracking move; familiar and unsettling at the same time

a shot where one impossible thing calmly exists in an ordinary, realistically filmed setting — clones, a living photograph, a mountain of bodies, a car on a lift in the desert — and people behave as if this were normal
a finger-sized person lives in the ordinary world — dances on a carpet, stands on fingertips, dangles as a keychain, climbs over a laptop, drags a giant bag; everyday objects turn into a landscape
a shot underwater — a blue-turquoise or colored murky medium, weightless hair and fabric, bubbles, a glowing surface above, a floating camera; in the edit also a "dive" with the sound going muffled

a subject or an object in an infinite empty space — an even black or white background without walls, horizon or details; all attention is on the figure, a sense of isolation, a dream or being "outside of time"
glitch sound — digital clicks, crackle and track stutters to go with glitch effects; this also covers a single click-tick, tape stop and record scratch
impact — a short low hit on a cut, a punch-in or the landing of a move: a click, a body falling in pitch and a tail; from a dry punch to a cinematic boom
riser — a building sound before an accent or a drop: noise or a tone sweeps upward, grows and cuts off exactly at the point of resolution (a hit, the drop, a cut, a title)
sub drop — a falling low-frequency rumble on the entry into the drop: a pure 70–150 Hz sine glides down to 24–40 Hz within fractions of a second, with harmonics so it reads on a phone
whoosh — a short moving noise that builds to a peak and fades away; for fast camera moves and transitions, with the sound peak on the cut or at the peak speed of the jerk
a digital shake of the whole frame on a beat or a hit — an impulse exactly on the transient frame and a decaying rebound over 0.15–0.3 s; micro, impact, heavy, rotational and "bass" variants
close-up — the face from forehead to chin (or an object, hands) fills almost the whole frame; emotion and reaction become the main event
extreme close-up — only part of the face (eyes, lips) or a detail of an object is in frame; it pins the eye to a single feature and makes for short rhythmic inserts

extreme wide shot — a landscape or a huge interior where a person or a car is a small dot, or absent altogether; scale, emptiness and place say more than the subject; the shot opens up the world, separates chapters and shows loneliness

medium close-up — head and shoulders down to mid-chest; the face reads, but gestures, clothing and a bit of the environment are visible — the workhorse shot for speech, dialogue and a reaction with a gesture
a close-up of the face at the moment it "dawns" on the subject — the eyes widen, the gaze drifts up or into the distance, while the camera slowly pushes in and the light on the face increases

a person (or a group) poses for the camera as if for a photo but is filmed on video — almost motionless, looking into the lens or past it, while the wind, breathing and the background stay alive; a series of such portraits tells about a place and its people

wide shot — the whole subject with the location around them; the shot answers the questions "where", "who stands where" and "how the subject relates to the space", so it opens scenes and gives the viewer back the geography
the camera stays in place and tilts up or down — the eye glides from one point of interest to another and reveals it (detail → face, top → people, face → hands)
a lightning-fast camera whip up or down with solid vertical motion blur — in half a second it throws the eye to a target above or below, or takes it out of the scene
a 0.25–1 s stretch of motion plays forward, then mirrored back to the starting pose, 1–4 times — the gesture "bounces" back and forth like a rubber band
time stops at the peak of the action — the subject and everything flying around it hang in the air, while the camera keeps moving around it or through the scene
the frame is frozen like a photograph, and only one zone — water, hair, steam, leaves — moves endlessly in an invisible 0.6–4 s loop; a pause, atmosphere, a stopped moment
a moving subject drags a trail of copies of its past positions (0.3–2 s) — the copies hang in the frame and catch up with it when it stops; dance, a strike, a walk, a trance
the action plays 2–10 times faster than real time — compresses routine and time, gives a comic jerkiness or the feeling that the world is rushing past a frozen character
the action suddenly stops on a single frame and holds for 0.5–3 s — captures the peak of an emotion or action, introduces a character, puts a full stop on a scene or the ending
aliases: character intro on a freeze frame

moves.what: a camera journey over a long distance, sped up 10–60 times — toward a landmark, around it or along a street; the anchor object holds at one point of the frame while the city, people and clouds rush past
deliberate heavy motion blur, as with a long exposure — everything that moves (or the whole frame on a camera jerk) stretches into streaks of 3–25 % of the frame; speed, chaos, dream, detachment
playback at 1/2–1/5 of real speed to stretch a peak of motion, a walk or an emotional beat, while the music keeps its normal tempo
fast–slow–fast inside one uncut shot: the footage rushes in, brakes hard into slow motion at the peak of the action, then rushes out again, so the motion itself keeps time with the music
the motion "breaks up" into 5–12 images per second — each phase freezes for 2–6 frames and is usually blurred, as with a long exposure; chaos, adrenaline, disorientation
extreme slowdown of 10–40 times or more — a hit, a wingbeat, a flash or a splash lasting fractions of a second stretches over several seconds and reveals details invisible to the eye

one static frame is cut into stripes, rays, rings or nested frames, and each slice shows its own time from a timelapse; the sky in a single frame smoothly passes from day to night, and in animation the slices flow like a wave of time
a static or barely moving shot in which minutes, hours or days pass in 2–6 seconds — clouds race, the sun sets, the city lights up, a flower opens, people appear and disappear

the clip's speed pulses on the beats of the track — on each beat the action peak almost freezes and is sharp, between beats the shot rushes by at ×4–8 with motion blur; a remap of a whole section to the beat, not a single ramp
the camera follows a subject who walks away from it at a constant distance — the viewer sees the back and the path ahead and seems to be walking along behind

the subject walks or rides straight toward the camera while the camera retreats ahead of them at the same speed — the face and the outfit stay in frame the whole time, while the space behind recedes into depth
a camera with no subject slowly wanders through a space like an invisible guest — drifting past people and details in a single take, turning its "gaze" now to one, now to another
the camera moves together with a walking or riding subject at the same speed — the subject is "glued" to one spot in the frame while the world flows past
a swap of place, partner or look hidden inside an orbit: when the arcing camera's blur, the subject's body or hair fills the frame, everything behind the subject is replaced
aliases: orbit the subject and land somewhere else

moves.what: one continuous camera move carries the viewer through 3 or more scenes in a row — new worlds are "docked" at the side (or nested inside a screen), the seams are hidden behind people, trees, posts and dark passes, and it feels like the move will never end

the outgoing shot fades out smoothly while the next one emerges on top of it over 0.6–2.6 s — a soft change of time, place or thought; in the match variant the main shapes of both frames sit in the same place

two (less often three) full frames are superimposed semi-transparently and live together for 1–5 s — a face and a landscape, a person and a second angle of them, a dream over reality; a dissolve whose middle is stretched into an image of its own
a fade to black or to white — the shot fades to black (or goes to white), a pause holds, and the next shot emerges from it; it puts a full stop, separates chapters, opens and closes the video
a flash on the cut — 1–4 frames of white or colored overexposure (or a short fade to white and back out of it) hide the join and hit the beat of the track; an accent hit, not a change of time

a cut the viewer does not notice — the camera moves into a "neutral" frame (darkness, fog, a cloud, a texture up close, an object filling the frame) or into a matching shape and comes out of it already in another scene, without stopping its motion
a graphic shape wipe — a circle, diamond, star, stripes or shards grow from a point (or shrink to a point) with a hard edge and reveal the next shot

a transition through optical distortion — over 5–9 frames the image bulges like a lens, gets pinched into a point or twists into a vortex around a single center, is blurred at the peak of the deformation and gives way to the next shot, which straightens out of the same deformation

a cut "through liquid" — the boundary between shots is organic — the new shot shows through in patches in the dark or bright areas of the old one, grows as a soft blot, or the whole frame melts into ripples like glass under water and the next shot assembles out of them

a subject or object turns into something else right in the frame — the new form spreads across the body, emerges under a change of light, flashes in with a strobe or swells up, while the background and the shot stay the same

one image flows smoothly into another — contours and features shift into the positions of the new object at the same time as the color changes; a transition between faces, objects, shapes, or a chain of such transformations
the outgoing frame behaves like a sheet of paper or a photo print — it folds back and falls, tears down the middle or crumples up and flies away, while the next shot is already playing underneath

a transition into another scene through an opening — the camera flies into a screen, a mouth, a pupil, a mirror, a hole or a door and comes out in a new place; or a pull-out shows that the scene was inside an object; or a rift window into another world opens right in the frame

a full-screen picture turns out to be the image on a device screen in the next shot (a phone, a TV, a monitor, a scoreboard) — or the other way round, a screen in the frame grows and its content becomes the new frame
a change of place without a cut — the subject stays put while the set around them physically goes away (sinks, rises, falls, slides apart, turns) and reveals a new environment
the outgoing frame breaks like a material — it cracks into glass shards in which the next shot is already visible, or crumbles into fine dust that the wind blows away, revealing the new scene

the camera tracks steadily sideways along a row of adjacent "cells" — train compartments, rooms, shops, lockers — and behind each wall or column a new scene, a new time or the same subject in a new state is revealed; several scenes are tied together by one continuous move
a cut inside a rotation of the frame around the lens axis — the outgoing shot spins up, the incoming one continues the rotation in the same direction and settles level

a cut hidden inside a sharp sideways jerk of the camera — the outgoing shot breaks into solid motion blur, the incoming one comes out of the same blur in the same direction and brakes on a new subject
a wipe — the boundary between shots travels across the frame, most often hidden by an object right at the lens (a passer-by, a column, palms, a back), behind which the new scene opens up
a cut at the peak of a sharp push-in — the outgoing shot accelerates into a detail, the frame blurs radially, and the next shot comes out of the same motion, braking on the new scene
the camera travels sideways parallel to the scene — next to a walking subject or along a row of people, a room, a shop window; the near passes faster than the far, and the space reads in layers
kinetic text to music — words and short lines land exactly on the track's beats, hit on downbeats and the kick and get denser toward the drop; timing comes from the beat grid, not the voice

on-screen text is built into the depth of the frame together with the subject — words stand behind them, burst out from behind their back, run as a line along their contour or circle an object as a ring; the subject overlaps the text and the frame looks like a cover

the list of the video's creators (role and name) at the start or at the end — as changing cards or as a column rolling up, on a black field or over the last calm shot; it closes the piece, credits the team and sets the signature style of the work

the text exists inside the world of the frame — printed on an object, written on a wall, emerging from the scene's material — and obeys the scene's perspective, light, motion and occlusions instead of hanging on the screen as a flat plate

the text looks drawn by hand — marker, brush, pen, chalk, puffy outlined letters; a word writes itself on screen letter by letter or stroke by stroke, boils, flows into the next word or stands as a handwritten caption; a warm, personal, homemade delivery

a short authorial caption that states the time, place, chapter, a line of dialogue or a prologue — as a line over the first frame of a scene or as a separate text card between shots; it switches the viewer to a new stretch of the story
karaoke captions — a short line stays in place while the word being spoken is highlighted by color, a box, a bounce or a fill exactly as it is said; the eye follows the voice
text becomes the main event of the frame — words and letters appear, jump, stretch, flip and replace each other in the rhythm of the voice or the music, 1–3 words per screen

a caption plate in the lower part of the frame — the speaker's name and role, a place or a topic — comes in half a second after their first shot, holds for 3–5 s and leaves neatly, without intruding on the interface zones or the subtitles

the narrator's handwritten notes right in the frame — amounts, labels, a calculation with an arrow and a total are typed out letter by letter in time with the speech next to the subject, old values get crossed out and corrected; the viewer sees the scene's bookkeeping or who is who

one word or a short phrase multiplies — as an echo stack, in rows, as a full-frame grid, as rays, on the surface of a cylinder — and the whole construction lives as a 1–4 s loop; the text becomes a pattern and a graphic insert

a line of text conveys speech or vocals in sync with the sound — at the bottom center or as lyrics in the middle of the frame, with changing phrases; the subtitle style (font, color, outline, position, delivery) itself becomes part of the video's aesthetic

the main title — the name of the video, the song or the subject, large, for 1–6 s, over a calm opening shot or on a separate card (black, colored, textured); a cover that announces the start or puts a full stop at the end

a main title or a character introduction title in the manner of 1920s–1970s cinema — the typeface, color, size and delivery of its era over the picture, often with film grain and gate weave; instantly sets an old-movie feel and the genre
a lightning-fast zoom-in from a wide or medium shot onto a face or a detail — in half a second, with motion blur and a hard landing
a zoom-in or zoom-out with a huge scale range (×10–×100 and more) — from a detail to a whole location or the reverse, cut together from several shots into one move
aliases: from wide shot to detail in one move

moves.what: smooth zoom-in toward the subject without changing the camera position — only the scale grows, perspective and parallax stay the same
a zoom-in and an immediate return to the original shot size, once or several times in rhythm — the frame "breathes" or "beats"
a continuous zoom-in that never ends — when the frame "runs out", it is replaced by the next one, nested in the center of the previous one
moving away from a detail or the subject to a wide shot that reveals the context — often with an unexpected element that was out of frame
an instant digital zoom-in of ×1.1–1.35 over 1–3 frames exactly on the beat — the shot size "snaps" on the hit and holds or springs back; an accent inside the shot without a cut
an almost imperceptible constant zoom-in (less often a zoom-out) over the whole shot — builds tension or intimacy without giving the camera away
aliases: bringing a static shot to life
